figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Answer quality for retrievers (grey), pooled across four QA datasets; comparison to an oracle (blue) selecting the best retriever per query. The retrievers are close to one another and all far below the oracle: a large room for improvement exists in choosing the best retriever per query at inference.
figures.headline: Individual retrievers score between 0.22 and 0.28 F1 while the per-query oracle reaches 0.75.
citing_sentences: Averaged over various datasets, the retrievers we study are close in performance ($0.22$ to $0.28$ answer F1), but an oracle that picks the right one for each query reaches $0.75$ F1, almost $3\times$ the best fixed retriever (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The formulation, end to end: each candidate mechanism retrieves an evidence set $D_{i}$; a shared reranker backbone scores each $(q,D_{i})$ pair in its own forward pass, reading the passages rather than the mechanism’s identity or confidence score; a comparison head with no mechanism-specific parameters reads $h_{1},\dots,h_{R}$ jointly; and the reader answers from the selected set $D_{\hat{r}}$. Supervision is the answer each evidence set yields (dashed, training only). Nothing in the pipeline changes if a mechanism is added, removed, or run on a different corpus.
figures.headline: A shared reranker scores each retriever's evidence, and a comparison head without retriever-specific parameters selects among them.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The reported population holds half of the gap to the oracle: the unfiltered test set split into three groups, by share of queries (top) and by share of the F1 gap between our router and the oracle (bottom). No answer: no retriever’s evidence yields a correct answer, so these queries add nothing to the gap. Near-tie: the two best retrievers are within $0.05$ F1 of each other. Routable: the two best retrievers differ by at least $0.05$; this is the population we report on, $18.7\%$ of queries holding $51.4\%$ of the gap.
figures.headline: Routable queries make up 18.7% of the test set and hold 51.4% of the remaining gap to the oracle.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 shows what this leaves out: on the unfiltered test set, no retriever answers $14.7\%$ of queries, and a further $66.7\%$ are near-ties between the two best retrievers; the remaining $18.7\%$ is the population we report on.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Generalizable routing: gain over each dataset’s best fixed retriever when that dataset (its queries and its corpus) is held out of training entirely. RAGCompass stays positive on all four; three query-only routers, held to the identical protocol on the identical rows, never exceed the best fixed retriever. Three seeds for every method; whiskers are one std.
figures.headline: RAGCompass stays above the best fixed retriever on all four held-out datasets, while three query-only routers never exceed it.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Query-only routers do not discriminate: how often each router selects the retriever held out of its training (three seeds, $\pm$ one std in each label). Shaded: the $14$–$26\%$ range of our head. On every fold the rate is within about three points of the rate on queries where the held-out retriever is the best choice.
figures.headline: Query-only routers select the held-out retriever at nearly the same rate whether or not it is the best choice.
citing_sentences: RAGCompass also generalizes by design: held out from an entire dataset and its corpus, RAGCompass retains more than $80\%$ of its in-distribution gain on some datasets (Figure 5).
All three query-only routers fail to improve (Figure 5).

None of these baselines discriminates between queries (Figure 5): their pick rates for the held-out retriever range from $0\%$ to $61\%$ across folds and stay nearly unchanged on the queries where it is the oracle choice, whereas our head picks it more often where it is right.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Recall improves clearly: retrieval recall@5 and nDCG@5 by method. Our recall gain is clear; the nDCG gain is small and roughly matched by the fusion baselines.
figures.headline: Routing lifts recall@5 clearly above fusion baselines, while its ranking-quality gain is small and roughly matched by them.
citing_sentences: That is $+5.0$ points of recall, ahead of both fusion baselines ($0.6853$ RRF, $0.6801$ MoR), and $+1.3$ of nDCG, roughly level with them ($0.6754$, $0.6800$; Figure 6).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Held-out tracks in-distribution: leave-one-dataset-out: the router trained without a dataset (“held out”) tracks the identical router trained with it (“in-distribution”) far more closely than either tracks the best fixed retriever, on every dataset where routing has headroom to begin with.
figures.headline: Held-out routers track in-distribution routers far more closely than either tracks the best fixed retriever.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Identity-free stays stable: cost of leaving one retriever out of training, relative to the all-five control. Each row pairs the two heads on the same held-out retriever, so the connector is the penalty the identity embedding pays. The identity-free head (blue) stays within $1.2$pp on every fold; the identity embedding (orange) is far more volatile, and its ColBERTv2 fold (red) crosses below the best-fixed floor – worse than not routing.
figures.headline: The identity-free head stays within 1.2pp of the control on every fold, while the identity embedding falls below best fixed on one.
citing_sentences: Figures 8 and Figure 8 show the visualization of the transfer results reported in Section 5.3.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Generalizes across depth: gain over the best fixed retriever at the trained depth ($k{=}5$) and at an unseen shallower depth ($k{=}3$), with no retraining. Each bar is measured against its own depth’s best fixed retriever; those are different systems, so the pairs share an axis but not a floor.
figures.headline: Routing gains over each depth's best fixed retriever at k=5 and unseen k=3, with no retraining.
citing_sentences: As a share of what is reachable the router captures $13.7\%$ against $16.3\%$ at its trained depth, and the per-dataset ordering is unchanged (Figure 9), with NQ the smallest at both depths ($+0.42$pp at $k{=}5$, negative at $k{=}3$).

abstract:
Different retrievers exist for retrieval-augmented generation, yet none performs best for all queries. Therefore, the key question is: given a query and retrieved passages from different retrievers, which one is most suited for that query? Existing routers usually make predictions from query-specific features and a fixed pool of retrievers; such routers have no output for an unseen retriever and are incapable by design on a new corpus. To fill these gaps, RAGCompass reads the retrieved passage sets themselves: passages from an unfamiliar retriever or corpus stay directly comparable to other passages, so routing stays well designed where a query-only map would fail. We contrastively fine-tune a reranker against the answer each evidence set produces, which accounts for most of the gain; a small comparison head adds a moderate improvement, and neither component has retriever-specific parameters. RAGCompass improves answer F1 by $28\%$ relative to the best fixed retriever, and outperforms fusion baselines, three query-only routers, and a prompted $8$B language model. Generalization experiments show that RAGCompass keeps most of its gain under an unseen corpus, retriever, or reader, while query-only baselines fall to the best fixed retriever or below.

Code is made available at https://github.com/Graph-COM/RAGCompass.

sections.body:
The introduction frames retriever routing: given a query and several retrievers, pick the one whose passages the reader should use. Averaged across datasets, the retrievers score between 0.22 and 0.28 answer F1, while an oracle that picks per query reaches 0.75, almost three times the best fixed retriever.

RAGCompass fine-tunes a reranker so that its score for each retriever's passages tracks the answer those passages produce. A comparison head then reads all candidates jointly. The reranker accounts for most of the gain, and the head adds 1.4pp. The paper reports a 28% relative improvement over the best fixed retriever. The routing decision adds about 0.2s to a 5-6s per-query pipeline, and running every candidate retriever first is the stated cost.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Retriever choice varies by query, and an oracle picking per query reaches 0.75 F1 against 0.28 for the best fixed retriever.

sections.body:
The related work groups prior routers by what they condition on. Reciprocal rank fusion and a mixture-of-retrievers baseline combine retrievers without learning from the retrieved evidence. Query performance prediction, the LTRR ranker, and ROUTERRETRIEVER predict retriever quality from query features, retrieval scores, or per-retriever embeddings. R3AG is closest in spirit: it uses language-model judgments of retrieved documents as training labels, but routes with one learned identity token per retriever.

Table 1 compares the formulations on whether they read evidence, compare candidates jointly, and hold up under an unseen corpus or mechanism. The authors state that to their knowledge none of these formulations has been tested under a shift.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior routers read queries or retriever identities rather than retrieved passages, and none was tested under a shift.

sections.body:
Each retriever's passage set receives a utility equal to the F1 of the answer the fixed reader writes from it, and routing selects the highest. The scorer is a Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B backbone that reads the query and one retriever's passages in its own forward pass and emits a yes-logit score. Training matches a softmax over scores to a softmax over utilities using KL divergence, which couples the candidates through shared normalization.

A two-layer transformer comparison head reads the backbone's hidden states for all retrievers jointly, with self-attention across retrievers. The backbone is fine-tuned first, and the head is then trained on its frozen representations. Neither part has parameters tied to a particular retriever.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Routing is cast as reranking evidence sets, with a reranker trained to match the answer F1 each set yields.

sections.body:
Four datasets are used: Natural Questions, MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA. Each query is routed among five retrievers: a dense retriever, BM25, SPLADE-v3, ColBERTv2, and HippoRAG2. Each supplies five passages to a fixed Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct reader. Only queries whose top two utilities differ by at least 0.05 are used. The metric is test answer F1, with recall@5 and nDCG@5 also reported for the routed choice. Splits are 70/30 and results average three seeds.

Three shifts are tested: leave-one-dataset-out for an unseen corpus, leave-one-retriever-out for an unseen mechanism, and a swap to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as an unseen reader. Baselines include rank fusion, a static-weight mixture, three learned query-only routers, majority vote, and a prompted language-model router.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Five retrievers are routed across four question-answering datasets, with generalization tested by holding out a dataset, a retriever, or the reader.

sections.body:
The fine-tuned scalar scorer reaches 0.3412 F1, and the comparison head brings RAGCompass to 0.3552. The scorer accounts for 6.3 of the 7.7pp gain, and the head adds 1.4pp against seed standard deviations of 0.3 to 0.6pp. The three query-only routers fall to or below the best fixed retriever. R3AG routes nearly all test queries to ColBERTv2.

Gains are uneven: roughly 12pp on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA, 4.8pp on MuSiQue, and 0.42pp on NQ. The routing decision adds 0.222s per query to a 5.687s retrieve-and-answer pipeline, which is 3.9%. A large oracle gap remains, with the oracle at 0.7508.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: RAGCompass reaches 0.3552 test F1, +7.7pp over the best fixed retriever and +3.5pp over the strongest baseline.

sections.body:
The discussion argues that the routing signal matters more than how candidate scores are coupled. Coupling through joint normalization moves the result less than seed noise, and comparing representations rather than scalars adds little. Reading all retrievers in one context underperforms per-retriever encoding.

The authors disagree with R3AG's use of a fixed identity token per retriever, and use the evidence retrieved for each particular query instead. They argue that reading evidence enables generalization, since a passage set stays comparable whatever produced it. The stated remaining limit is the oracle gap, 0.7508 against 0.3552, with the router matching the oracle on about a third of queries.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Utility supervision beats relevance supervision by 2.11pp, while score coupling changes results by less than seed noise.

sections.body:
The conclusion restates the problem as a content-grounded comparison supervised by downstream utility, rather than as prediction of each retriever's quality from other signals. RAGCompass uses a fine-tuned reranker as scorer and a comparison head, and neither has parameters tied to a retriever. It outperforms every router compared on answer F1, at 3.9% of the cost of the generation pipeline.

Most of the gain comes from the utility-supervised reranker, and the head adds a small further improvement. The method keeps most of its advantage on a corpus, retriever, or reader it never saw in training, while the query-only routers do not exceed the best fixed retriever. Narrowing the remaining gap to the oracle is left for future work.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: RAGCompass outperforms every compared router at 3.9% of generation pipeline cost and keeps most of its gain under unseen conditions.

sections.body:
The utility target is defined through one reader, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and one retrieval depth of five. The reader swap tests exactly one alternative. Depth is tested only in the shallower direction, since going deeper would require re-running retrieval and regenerating every label. Every result uses one backbone size, Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B.

The three learned query-only baselines are reimplementations that may differ from the originals, and MoR is simplified to one validation-fitted weight per retriever. The 3.9% overhead covers only the routing decision, on one L40S device at one batch size. It excludes running all R retrievers, which is parallelizable but a real cost, and the figure should be read as an order of magnitude.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Results rest on one reader, one retrieval depth, one backbone scale, and reimplemented baselines, so transfer is untested beyond those.

sections.body:
Joint-prompt encodings reach 0.2735 to 0.2942, below the per-retriever pipeline's 0.3552. The head sweep saturates near 0.353 on frozen backbones, and end-to-end training reaches 0.3623. The routed choice reaches recall@5 of 0.7253 against 0.6749 for the best single retriever. Majority vote reaches 0.2009.

At retrieval depth k=3 with no retraining, the router reaches 0.3343 against 0.2979 for the best fixed retriever, a gain of +3.64pp. A prompted language model gains at most 3.20pp, and its evidence-judging variant takes 0.358s per query. Estimated compute is about 700 GPU-hours on NVIDIA L40S GPUs.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers encoding and head ablations, retrieval metrics, majority vote, depth and data-size checks, baseline details, per-dataset results, and language-model router costs.
